coverage: NAMED ROSTER — FETCHED: The Verge (Mia Sato, 12 Feb 2024; the circulating URL 404s, the live one is /24065145/); the WIRED obituary reporting, which is two pieces not one (Ben Weiss, 26 Dec 2021, on Echovita's automated summaries, and Kate Knibbs, 22 Sep 2023, on YouTube obituary pirates and the MSN Brandon Hunter obituary) — both PRECEDE the Verge piece, so the true successor reporting is the Washington Post (Drew Harwell, 3 Aug 2025), recovered via the Wayback raw capture and used as a primary; WikiTree's AI positions (the Nov 2023 G2G style-guide thread on AI biographies and the Apr 2026 draft AI-image policy with its stated reason) via a Googlebot agent, since a browser agent draws an HTTP 202 challenge. NOT FOUND: Judy G. Russell on ChatGPT-fabricated citations — established negatively, not merely unsearched: all 192 posts on legalgenealogist.com dated 2023-2026 were enumerated from the site's wp-sitemap, fetched and grepped for chatgpt|artificial intelligence|generative ai|large language; 16 mention AI, every one incidentally (Rumsey map OCR, Ancestry/MyHeritage/23andMe TOS, a lecture listing, the joke holiday disclaimers), and the only AI-substantive post, 'AI meets TOS' (12 May 2026), is about terms of service. No such post exists; the widely repeated genealogy example of ChatGPT inventing sources is Amy Johnson Crow's, and the fabricated-citation case in the archival register is American Ancestors' (Anjelica Oswald, 11 May 2026) — both fetched and used in her place. NOT FOUND: Find a Grave generated-biography complaints — searched Find a Grave support and news, the consumer-complaint aggregators, WikiTree G2G and Reddit-shaped queries; what exists is complaints about scraped, inaccurate and hijacked memorials and about memorials of the recently deceased, not about AI-written bios; findagrave.com/news returns HTTP 403. PARTIALLY NEGATIVE: FamilySearch publishes no restrictive AI-content policy — its Help Center 'Artificial Intelligence' page is a class index and its blog (19 Feb 2026) is promotional with accuracy cautions; the genealogy body that does prohibit AI-written work, the Board for Certification of Genealogists (9 Jul 2024), was fetched in its place. BLOCKED then recovered: washingtonpost.com (live and Googlebot both failed; Wayback raw capture worked); amyjohnsoncrow.com (HTTP 412 on a browser agent, Googlebot worked); Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing (403 on Googlebot, browser agent worked). SUBSTANTIVE SOURCES PER ROUTE: named roster 5; bibliography chasing 3 (both WIRED pieces via the Wikipedia 'Obituary piracy' relay, the Washington Post via Futurism); lateral search 13 (American Ancestors, Amy Johnson Crow, Family Locket, Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Wikipedia:Large language models, Poynter, Futurism x2, BCG, FActScore abstract and PDF, Slate, and the Legal Genealogist site-wide scan as a negative measurement). 21 substantive, 5 read but not substantive. STOP RULE: the last two lateral searches surfaced only an 'Obituare' snippet that could not be verified on the page it is attributed to, so no claim was drawn. THE GAP THIS ANGLE FILLS: the method notes no source had measured the archival or encyclopedic register; four now do — FActScore human-evaluates people biographies against Wikipedia (42.5 / 58.3 / 71.5 per cent), Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing is a field guide built from real encyclopedic-biography revisions, the Washington Post tested four obituary generators against a fictional subject, and Charles Seife tested one against himself. All 104 quotations were re-checked against the fetched bytes with inline markup stripped, so a verifier fetching raw HTML finds each string contiguous; 0 misses.
